# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

<!-- END EXACT SPEC toy/spec/stage-1.md -->

# `toy` — stage 2: one page, one button

Keep the stage 1 API working. The deliverable is unchanged: the service source, a
`Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory, and the command in `RUN.md`
builds and starts the service with no manual steps.

Add a page at `/` with these two elements:

| `data-testid` | Element |
|---|---|
| `counter-value` | Visible text containing only the current integer, e.g. `7` |
| `increment-button` | A button that adds 1 |

On page load, read the value from `GET /counter`. Clicking the button calls
`POST /counter/increment` once and displays the returned value. Reloading the page
shows the server's current value, including increments made by another client.

Any layout is fine. Serve all assets from the container; no CDN is available at run
time. Elements are located by the exact `data-testid` values above and by nothing else.

Stage 1 must still pass.

<!-- END EXACT SPEC toy/spec/stage-2.md -->

<!-- BEGIN EXACT SPEC toy/spec/stage-3.md -->
# `toy` — stage 3: no lost increments

No new endpoints and no new page elements. Stages 1 and 2 must still pass, unchanged.
What changes is the load: the same API is now called by many clients at the same
moment, and every call has to count.

## Concurrent increments

When 20 clients increment together, all 20 requests must return 200 and the counter
must increase by exactly 20. Each response returns the value immediately after its
own increment: starting at 7, the responses contain each integer from 8 through 27
exactly once, in any arrival order. No transport errors or 5xx responses are allowed.

The burst is repeated three times, from both zero and a nonzero seed.

Reading the value, adding one, and storing it is one operation, not three. Protect it
with a lock or use an atomic database update. Two requests that read the same number
and write the same number have lost an increment, and the final read will show it.

<!-- END EXACT SPEC toy/spec/stage-3.md -->

<!-- BEGIN EXACT SPEC toy/spec/stage-4.md -->
# `toy` — stage 4: increment by a chosen amount

Stages 1, 2 and 3 must still pass, and that is most of the work.

`POST /counter/increment` accepts an optional `by` in its request body:

| Request body | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `{"by": 5}` from 7 | `200 {"value":12}` | Adds 5 |
| absent, `{}`, or `{"by": 1}` | `200 {"value":8}` | Adds 1, exactly as before |
| `{"by": 0}`, `{"by": -1}`, `{"by": "5"}` | `400`, any body | None — the value does not move |

`by` is an integer of 1 or more. Zero, a negative number, a string and a fraction are
all rejected with `400` and change nothing; the next request works normally. A request
with no body, or with `{}`, still means 1, which is why stages 1 to 3 keep behaving
identically.

The page from stage 2 is unchanged: its button still adds 1.

> **The stage-3 rule is the same in words and wider in effect:** nothing may be lost
> when 20 clients increment together. It now covers amounts, not just counts. Twenty
> clients sending `by` of 1 through 20 move the counter by exactly 210, and no two of
> them may be told the same value.

If the amount is added outside the lock, or read before the lock and written after it,
this is where it shows.

<!-- END EXACT SPEC toy/spec/stage-4.md -->

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 3: no lost increments

No new endpoints and no new page elements. Stages 1 and 2 must still pass, unchanged.
What changes is the load: the same API is now called by many clients at the same
moment, and every call has to count.

## Concurrent increments

When 20 clients increment together, all 20 requests must return 200 and the counter
must increase by exactly 20. Each response returns the value immediately after its
own increment: starting at 7, the responses contain each integer from 8 through 27
exactly once, in any arrival order. No transport errors or 5xx responses are allowed.

The burst is repeated three times, from both zero and a nonzero seed.

Reading the value, adding one, and storing it is one operation, not three. Protect it
with a lock or use an atomic database update. Two requests that read the same number
and write the same number have lost an increment, and the final read will show it.

# `toy` — stage 4: increment by a chosen amount

Stages 1, 2 and 3 must still pass, and that is most of the work.

`POST /counter/increment` accepts an optional `by` in its request body:

| Request body | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `{"by": 5}` from 7 | `200 {"value":12}` | Adds 5 |
| absent, `{}`, or `{"by": 1}` | `200 {"value":8}` | Adds 1, exactly as before |
| `{"by": 0}`, `{"by": -1}`, `{"by": "5"}` | `400`, any body | None — the value does not move |

`by` is an integer of 1 or more. Zero, a negative number, a string and a fraction are
all rejected with `400` and change nothing; the next request works normally. A request
with no body, or with `{}`, still means 1, which is why stages 1 to 3 keep behaving
identically.

The page from stage 2 is unchanged: its button still adds 1.

> **The stage-3 rule is the same in words and wider in effect:** nothing may be lost
> when 20 clients increment together. It now covers amounts, not just counts. Twenty
> clients sending `by` of 1 through 20 move the counter by exactly 210, and no two of
> them may be told the same value.

If the amount is added outside the lock, or read before the lock and written after it,
this is where it shows.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 3: no lost increments

No new endpoints and no new page elements. Stages 1 and 2 must still pass, unchanged.
What changes is the load: the same API is now called by many clients at the same
moment, and every call has to count.

## Concurrent increments

When 20 clients increment together, all 20 requests must return 200 and the counter
must increase by exactly 20. Each response returns the value immediately after its
own increment: starting at 7, the responses contain each integer from 8 through 27
exactly once, in any arrival order. No transport errors or 5xx responses are allowed.

The burst is repeated three times, from both zero and a nonzero seed.

Reading the value, adding one, and storing it is one operation, not three. Protect it
with a lock or use an atomic database update. Two requests that read the same number
and write the same number have lost an increment, and the final read will show it.

## Mechanisms and consequences

Use Python 3.12 standard library: one process, ThreadingHTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler, json, threading.Lock. Set request_queue_size to 128 explicitly, sufficient to queue the specified 20 simultaneous clients without relying on the smaller server default. A single integer initialized to zero and a single lock belong to the server, shared across all handlers. No framework, database, Redis, accounts, tokens, workers, background polling, or runtime network services. This avoids deployment and synchronization dependencies; state deliberately disappears on process restart. Multiple processes or replicas are outside this contract because their memory would diverge.

All counter reads, resets and increments acquire the same lock. An increment adds and copies its returned integer while holding that lock. Serialize and write the captured result after releasing the lock; do not read shared state again when constructing the response. Reset replaces the sole integer before returning 204. Parse and validate bodies before mutation. Never hold the lock while reading request bytes or writing to a client. Response arrival order may differ from operation order; distinct operation results remain correct. Threading without an explicit lock or relying on the GIL is rejected because read/add/store must be one indivisible operation.

Stage 1 may use this safe foundation immediately. Scope discipline prohibits future UI or stage-4 amount behavior from being copied backward, not basic correctness. Stage 3 can make concurrency a tested guarantee without intentionally weakening earlier stages.

## HTTP and UI contract

Bind 0.0.0.0; PORT defaults to 8080. GET /health returns 200 JSON {"status":"ok"}. GET /counter returns 200 JSON {"value": current_integer} without mutation. POST /counter/increment in stages 1–3 accepts an absent body or {} and increments exactly once by 1; every request is independent. POST /_test/reset accepts the valid fixture object with integer value 0..1000000, synchronously replaces all state and returns 204 with zero body bytes. JSON responses carry application/json (optional UTF-8 charset); use explicit Content-Length for all responses and zero for reset. Read Content-Length bytes when a body is present. Return controlled 400 errors for malformed JSON/non-object bodies, with no mutation; such extra error behavior must not change required valid requests. GET /counter should send Cache-Control: no-store.

Stage 2 serves a self-contained page at / with all HTML/CSS/JS in the image, no CDN. Visible data-testid=counter-value contains only the server integer; data-testid=increment-button is a real button. Load GET /counter before enabling increments. Each accepted click issues one POST with {} and renders its returned value. Disable the button while its request is pending to avoid stale response races; never automatically retry a POST after an uncertain network failure because every request counts. Reload fetches server state, including other clients' increments. No localStorage, optimistic increments, or client-authoritative value. Loading/error explanation, if used, stays outside counter-value. Designer owns visual treatment and should preserve these semantics. Stage 3 adds no endpoints/elements; stage 4 leaves the page and its +1 request unchanged.

Only stage 4 interprets optional by: absent body, {} or missing by means 1. Validate type(by) is int and by >= 1; bool is not accepted as an integer. Zero, negatives, strings and fractional values return 400 and leave the integer unchanged; the next valid request works. Add the validated amount inside the existing critical section and capture the result there. Do not coerce strings, truncate floats, or impose a specification-invented business maximum.

Build from python:3.12-slim, use no third-party dependencies, copy explicit stage files, start python server.py with exec-form CMD. Do not download anything at service startup. # `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 3: no lost increments

No new endpoints and no new page elements. Stages 1 and 2 must still pass, unchanged.
What changes is the load: the same API is now called by many clients at the same
moment, and every call has to count.

## Concurrent increments

When 20 clients increment together, all 20 requests must return 200 and the counter
must increase by exactly 20. Each response returns the value immediately after its
own increment: starting at 7, the responses contain each integer from 8 through 27
exactly once, in any arrival order. No transport errors or 5xx responses are allowed.

The burst is repeated three times, from both zero and a nonzero seed.

Reading the value, adding one, and storing it is one operation, not three. Protect it
with a lock or use an atomic database update. Two requests that read the same number
and write the same number have lost an increment, and the final read will show it.

# `toy` — stage 4: increment by a chosen amount

Stages 1, 2 and 3 must still pass, and that is most of the work.

`POST /counter/increment` accepts an optional `by` in its request body:

| Request body | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `{"by": 5}` from 7 | `200 {"value":12}` | Adds 5 |
| absent, `{}`, or `{"by": 1}` | `200 {"value":8}` | Adds 1, exactly as before |
| `{"by": 0}`, `{"by": -1}`, `{"by": "5"}` | `400`, any body | None — the value does not move |

`by` is an integer of 1 or more. Zero, a negative number, a string and a fraction are
all rejected with `400` and change nothing; the next request works normally. A request
with no body, or with `{}`, still means 1, which is why stages 1 to 3 keep behaving
identically.

The page from stage 2 is unchanged: its button still adds 1.

> **The stage-3 rule is the same in words and wider in effect:** nothing may be lost
> when 20 clients increment together. It now covers amounts, not just counts. Twenty
> clients sending `by` of 1 through 20 move the counter by exactly 210, and no two of
> them may be told the same value.

If the amount is added outside the lock, or read before the lock and written after it,
this is where it shows.

## Mechanisms and consequences

Use Python 3.12 standard library: one process, ThreadingHTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler, json, threading.Lock. Set request_queue_size to 128 explicitly, sufficient to queue the specified 20 simultaneous clients without relying on the smaller server default. A single integer initialized to zero and a single lock belong to the server, shared across all handlers. No framework, database, Redis, accounts, tokens, workers, background polling, or runtime network services. This avoids deployment and synchronization dependencies; state deliberately disappears on process restart. Multiple processes or replicas are outside this contract because their memory would diverge.

All counter reads, resets and increments acquire the same lock. An increment adds and copies its returned integer while holding that lock. Serialize and write the captured result after releasing the lock; do not read shared state again when constructing the response. Reset replaces the sole integer before returning 204. Parse and validate bodies before mutation. Never hold the lock while reading request bytes or writing to a client. Response arrival order may differ from operation order; distinct operation results remain correct. Threading without an explicit lock or relying on the GIL is rejected because read/add/store must be one indivisible operation.

Stage 1 may use this safe foundation immediately. Scope discipline prohibits future UI or stage-4 amount behavior from being copied backward, not basic correctness. Stage 3 can make concurrency a tested guarantee without intentionally weakening earlier stages.

## HTTP and UI contract

JSON responses carry application/json (optional UTF-8 charset); use explicit Content-Length for all responses and zero for reset. Read Content-Length bytes when a body is present. # `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|

| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |

increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

| `increment-button` | A button that adds 1 |

On page load, read the value from `GET /counter`. Clicking the button calls

Any layout is fine. Serve all assets from the container; no CDN is available at run
time. Elements are located by the exact `data-testid` values above and by nothing else.

Stage 1 must still pass.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 2: one page, one button

Keep the stage 1 API working. The deliverable is unchanged: the service source, a
`Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory, and the command in `RUN.md`
builds and starts the service with no manual steps.

Add a page at `/` with these two elements:

| `data-testid` | Element |
|---|---|
| `counter-value` | Visible text containing only the current integer, e.g. `7` |
| `increment-button` | A button that adds 1 |

On page load, read the value from `GET /counter`. Clicking the button calls
`POST /counter/increment` once and displays the returned value. Reloading the page
shows the server's current value, including increments made by another client.

Any layout is fine. Serve all assets from the container; no CDN is available at run
time. Elements are located by the exact `data-testid` values above and by nothing else.

Stage 1 must still pass.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

Repository: /Users/frank/mygit/Tablekeeper/rehearsal/toy-result.
Source reference: /Users/frank/mygit/Tablekeeper/challenge at 803560d2a678ace1414465c098eb0ab5380ffade.
No implementation candidate exists; inspected revision is the accepted stage-1 baseline, not a rendered stage-2 candidate.

## Required implementation contract

Create standalone stage-2 sibling by copying accepted stage-1, preserving stage-1 files unchanged. Stage-2 has its own service, Dockerfile, RUN.md and local assets, without cross-folder imports or runtime internet. Python 3.12 standard library ThreadingHTTPServer retains shared lock, backlog 128, captured increment result, public JSON API and reset semantics. Start at zero; bind 0.0.0.0, PORT defaults 8080. Preserve GET /health, GET /counter, POST /counter/increment accepting empty or {}, and synchronous POST /_test/reset with valid integer seeds 0–1000000 and empty 204. Keep build/start one-command instructions, container constraints 2 CPUs/2 GiB, health within 60 seconds, requests within 5 seconds (reset 10). Stage 1 must still pass. Stage 3 must change no page elements; stage 4 must retain page +1 behavior.

At GET /, use one main landmark, h1 “Shared counter”, visible label “Current value”, one text element data-testid="counter-value", and native button type="button" data-testid="increment-button" labelled “Add 1”. The numeric element contains only unformatted integer text: no comma, suffix, label, spinner, or placeholder dash. A separate status paragraph and footer explain state and sharing. Static footer: “Shared across browsers. Reload to see the latest value.” Do not imply continuous synchronization.

On initial page load fetch GET /counter before enabling increment. Validate HTTP success and integer value before display. Exactly one POST /counter/increment with JSON {} per accepted activation. Set the pending guard synchronously before awaiting fetch; disable the native button while pending. On success display the returned value (do not compute locally), then re-enable. No optimistic values, POST retries, polling, storage, CDN, or remote fonts. Reload always fetches current shared state.

## States and microcopy

Loading: reserve the number's height but leave its contents empty/hidden until first successful read; never invent zero. Disable Add 1. Separate status “Loading counter…”.
Ready: show server integer, enable Add 1, clear transient status. Zero is a valid successful value, not an empty state.
Pending: retain last confirmed integer, disable Add 1, status “Adding 1…”. No animated count interpolation.
Success: replace numeric text with returned integer, enable Add 1, announce “Counter is now {value}.” in separate polite status region.
Initial read error (HTTP, malformed response, network or timeout): number remains empty; button disabled; status “Could not load the counter. Reload this page to try again.”
Increment failure or uncertain completion (HTTP, malformed response, network or timeout): preserve last confirmed integer, button disabled; status “Could not confirm the update. The number shown is the last confirmed value. Reload this page to check the current value.” Do not say the increment failed to happen. Browser reload is recovery; do not add a second action or auto-repeat POST.
Bound requests with a 10-second client AbortController timeout so a disconnected request cannot leave perpetual pending. A timed-out POST remains uncertain even after abort. Clear the timer after settlement.
Use one role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" region for all feedback; do not make the numeric element a duplicate live region. Native disabled plus textual status communicates state without relying on color. Keep keyboard focus where possible, never autofocus or force focus on status; after successful native-button activation verify continued keyboard usability.

## Visual decision (presentation choices, not additional product scope)

Direction: a small printed tally card, restrained cream and ink with an orange action. No dashboard navigation, extra controls, decorative graphics, framework, or animation required.
Tokens: --paper #F6F1E7; --surface #FFFCF5; --ink #24241F; --muted #59594F; --accent #A83D20; --accent-hover #873019; --border #C8C1B3; --focus #174EA6; --error #8A261D. Use ink on paper/surface and white on accent; disabled button uses surface with muted text and a clear border (avoid low-opacity whole-button styling). Error text uses error color plus explicit words. Verify measured contrast in candidate review (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text/control boundaries when needed).
Typography: Georgia, serif for heading; ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, monospace for number; Verdana, sans-serif for body/button. Local installed fallback fonts only. Heading 30–36px; number clamp(3rem, 12vw, 5rem), line-height 1.1 with tabular numerals; body 16px/1.5; footer 14px/1.5. Number can wrap anywhere for unusually long values rather than overflow; no ellipsis or clipping.
Spacing scale: 8, 16, 24, 32, 48px. Page min-height 100svh; content max-width 440px centered horizontally, natural vertical scroll, outer padding 24px (16px below 480px). Card uses 32px padding (24px mobile), 1px border, 12px radius and no mandatory shadow. Heading above number; generous 32px gap before action. Button full width, min-height 48px, 8px radius, bold 16px label. Reserve at least two lines for normal status; allow error text to expand naturally. Focus-visible: 3px solid focus token with 3px offset. Hover changes accent; active can darken without movement. No motion means reduced-motion preference is naturally honored.

## Acceptance checks for the committed candidate

At 360x800 and 1280x800 in an actual browser: page hierarchy legible, number and Add 1 initially visible when loaded, no horizontal overflow; errors wrap without overlap. At 320 CSS pixels / 200% text zoom, controls and feedback remain reachable and unclipped with vertical scrolling allowed.
Keyboard: Tab finds enabled native Add 1 with clear focus; Enter and Space each produce one POST when ready; pending disables repeat activation; usability returns after success. Accessible names and heading/main structure are present. Test color contrast rather than inferring PASS from token selection.
Observe initial GET before enabled action; seed 7 then reload shows only 7; activate once yields only 8; another client increment followed by reload shows 9. Inspect network for exactly one POST per accepted click. Delay response to observe pending and prevent double-click races. Exercise failed initial GET, failed/invalid POST response and disconnected/timed-out response; failure and uncertainty remain visible outside the numeric selector and cannot auto-repeat a POST.
Confirm local asset loading without external requests, unchanged stage-1 API suite, standalone stage-2 container, custom PORT and offline runtime in appropriate implementation/QA checks.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

|---|---|
| `counter-value` | Visible text containing only the current integer, e.g. `7` |

On page load, read the value from `GET /counter`. Clicking the button calls
`POST /counter/increment` once and displays the returned value. Reloading the page

Any layout is fine. Serve all assets from the container; no CDN is available at run
time. Elements are located by the exact `data-testid` values above and by nothing else.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

## States and microcopy

Loading: reserve the number's height but leave its contents empty/hidden until first successful read; never invent zero. Disable Add 1. Separate status “Loading counter…”.
Ready: show server integer, enable Add 1, clear transient status. Zero is a valid successful value, not an empty state.
Pending: retain last confirmed integer, disable Add 1, status “Adding 1…”. No animated count interpolation.
Success: replace numeric text with returned integer, enable Add 1, announce “Counter is now {value}.” in separate polite status region.
Initial read error (HTTP, malformed response, network or timeout): number remains empty; button disabled; status “Could not load the counter. Reload this page to try again.”
Increment failure or uncertain completion (HTTP, malformed response, network or timeout): preserve last confirmed integer, button disabled; status “Could not confirm the update. The number shown is the last confirmed value. Reload this page to check the current value.” Do not say the increment failed to happen. Browser reload is recovery; do not add a second action or auto-repeat POST.
Bound requests with a 10-second client AbortController timeout so a disconnected request cannot leave perpetual pending. A timed-out POST remains uncertain even after abort. Clear the timer after settlement.
Use one role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true" region for all feedback; do not make the numeric element a duplicate live region. Native disabled plus textual status communicates state without relying on color. Keep keyboard focus where possible, never autofocus or force focus on status; after successful native-button activation verify continued keyboard usability.

## States and microcopy

Loading: reserve the number's height but leave its contents empty/hidden until first successful read; never invent zero. Disable Add 1. Separate status “Loading counter…”.
Ready: show server integer, enable Add 1, clear transient status. Zero is a valid successful value, not an empty state.
Pending: retain last confirmed integer, disable Add 1, status “Adding 1…”. No animated count interpolation.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

| `data-testid` | Element |
|---|---|

| `increment-button` | A button that adds 1 |

On page load, read the value from `GET /counter`. Clicking the button calls
`POST /counter/increment` once and displays the returned value. Reloading the page
shows the server's current value, including increments made by another client.

# `toy` — stage 3: no lost increments

No new endpoints and no new page elements. Stages 1 and 2 must still pass, unchanged.
What changes is the load: the same API is now called by many clients at the same
moment, and every call has to count.

## Concurrent increments

When 20 clients increment together, all 20 requests must return 200 and the counter
must increase by exactly 20. Each response returns the value immediately after its
own increment: starting at 7, the responses contain each integer from 8 through 27
exactly once, in any arrival order. No transport errors or 5xx responses are allowed.

The burst is repeated three times, from both zero and a nonzero seed.

Reading the value, adding one, and storing it is one operation, not three. Protect it
with a lock or use an atomic database update. Two requests that read the same number
and write the same number have lost an increment, and the final read will show it.

EXACT STAGE 1 SPEC:
# `toy` — stage 1: a shared counter

Build a tiny HTTP service that stores one number. This practice exercise is unscored; it
exists to run the whole build-and-deliver loop once on something small.

## Deliverable

Create the service source, a `Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory.
The command in `RUN.md` must build and start the service with no manual steps.
Stage 1 needs only an API. Any language or framework is fine; memory-only storage is
fine. The counter starts at **0** when the service starts.

Bind `0.0.0.0` and read the listening port from `PORT`, defaulting to `8080`.
Your `Dockerfile` is built and the container started, with up to 60 seconds to become
healthy. Limits: 2 CPUs, 2 GiB memory, 5 seconds per request (10 for reset).
Install dependencies during the Docker build; no internet is available at run time.

## Four endpoints

All endpoints are public. JSON responses use `Content-Type: application/json`;
adding `charset=utf-8` is fine.

| Request | Response | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `200 {"status":"ok"}` | None |
| `GET /counter` | `200 {"value":0}` | Returns the current value; does not change it |
| `POST /counter/increment` | `200 {"value":1}` | Adds exactly 1 and returns the new value |
| `POST /_test/reset` with `{"value":7}` | `204`, empty body | Replaces the value with 7 |

The numbers above are examples. All clients share the same counter. Two successive
increments from 7 return 8, then 9; the next read returns 9.

Increment accepts an empty request body or `{}`. Every request is a new increment.
Reset is synchronous: once it returns, the next read must see the seeded value.
Reset fixtures are always valid: an object with an integer `value` between 0 and
1,000,000. Reset is called repeatedly, and no earlier state may remain.

There are no accounts, passwords, tokens, idempotency keys, or database requirements.

EXACT STAGE 2 SPEC:
# `toy` — stage 2: one page, one button

Keep the stage 1 API working. The deliverable is unchanged: the service source, a
`Dockerfile`, and a short `RUN.md` in one directory, and the command in `RUN.md`
builds and starts the service with no manual steps.

Add a page at `/` with these two elements:

| `data-testid` | Element |
|---|---|
| `counter-value` | Visible text containing only the current integer, e.g. `7` |
| `increment-button` | A button that adds 1 |

On page load, read the value from `GET /counter`. Clicking the button calls
`POST /counter/increment` once and displays the returned value. Reloading the page
shows the server's current value, including increments made by another client.

Any layout is fine. Serve all assets from the container; no CDN is available at run
time. Elements are located by the exact `data-testid` values above and by nothing else.

Stage 1 must still pass.

EXACT STAGE 3 SPEC:
# `toy` — stage 3: no lost increments

No new endpoints and no new page elements. Stages 1 and 2 must still pass, unchanged.
What changes is the load: the same API is now called by many clients at the same
moment, and every call has to count.

## Concurrent increments

When 20 clients increment together, all 20 requests must return 200 and the counter
must increase by exactly 20. Each response returns the value immediately after its
own increment: starting at 7, the responses contain each integer from 8 through 27
exactly once, in any arrival order. No transport errors or 5xx responses are allowed.

The burst is repeated three times, from both zero and a nonzero seed.

Reading the value, adding one, and storing it is one operation, not three. Protect it
with a lock or use an atomic database update. Two requests that read the same number
and write the same number have lost an increment, and the final read will show it.
